question:
What word does Chaucer NOT make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess?

Answer Choices:
A. Wente
B. Here
C. Fool
D. Hool
E. Countour
F. None of the above

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Hool

In the seven-line ababbcc stanzas of The Book of the Duchess Chaucer
regularly uses all of the other items as rhyme words.

* wente is regularly brought into the a-b couplet, e.g. wente : sente;
* here is used as a rhyme-position ending, e.g. here : fere/dere;
* fool is a normal –ool rhyme position in the poem, e.g. fool : cool/tool;
* countour ~ counter is used in the descriptive/contouring passages and is
rhymed with its normal Middle English partners, e.g. countour : mountour/
doubtour.

“Hool” in the sense in which it is offered here is not set up as a rhyme
partner in the poem. The –ool rhyme is carried by fool/cool/tool etc.,
and the form hool does not occur as a rhymed line ending in The Book of
the Duchess. That is the item of the five that Chaucer does not make a
rhyme with.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the rhyme-coupled dream-Book Chaucer is constantly using the ordinary
Middle English rhyme words

* wente ~ tente/sente
* here ~ there/where/ere
* fool ~ cool
* hool ~ cool/fool

in the normal Middle English couplet rhymes of the poem.  The
lexeme countour ~ counter ~ ‘ reckoner, account’ does not occur in the
poem as a rhyming word, so it is the only item in the list with which he
has no rhyme in The Book of the Duchess.  If the spelling variation is
normalised the four ordinary rhyme words are all attested in the poem,
hence the only non-rhymed item is countour.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour. The tempting choice is C, but in Book of the Duchess the Fool/Hool pair does occur as a rhyme in the Black Knight’s complaint, so Chaucer does make a rhyme with both Fool and Hool. Wente and Here also show up in line-final rhyme positions, such as Wente/entente and Here/manere. Countour is the odd one: it appears only mid-line as a common noun, not as a rhyming word in the poem. So the word he does NOT make a rhyme with is Countour.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. None of the above

All five of the forms occur as rhyming end-words in the Duchess. 

* wente ~ sente / wente is the normal past of wende and is used as a couplet rhyme throughout the dream-vision, e.g. wente : sente.
* here ~ dere / fere : the locative/demonstrative here is a regular rhyme in the octosyllabic couplets.
* fool ~ coole / tool : the narrator’s self-mockery is couched in a foil-fool couplet.
* hool ~ fool : hool / hole / whole is the Middle English form that Chaucer actually plays against fool in the same rhyme family, so hool is rhymed, indeed with fool itself.
* countour ~ mountour : the “countour” of a body/figure is used in the description of the Black Knight’s lady and is rhymed in the ordinary couplets.

Hence every item A–E is attested as a rhymed line-end in The Book of the Duchess, so none of them is a non-rhyming item.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the rhyming couplets of The Book of the Duchess Chaucer regularly brings to
line-end the words you list and pairs them in the normal Middle-English way.

* wente – e.g. wente / shente, wente / sente
* here – e.g. here / there, here / dere
* fool – e.g. fool / cool, fool / hool
* hool = ‘whole’ – the pair fool / hool is the familiar Chaucerian
fool-hool rhyme

The form countour / counteour does not occur as a rhyme-word, i.e. as a
line-final rhyme, in the Duchess. The word is not brought into the couplet
rhyme system of the poem, whereas the four other forms are. That is the
one item on the list which Chaucer never sets up as a rhyme in the work.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour. In Book of the Duchess, wente, here, fool, and hool all appear in end-rhyme positions—e.g., wente is paired with entente in the dream/hunt sequence, here with the usual Middle English -ere rhymes, and fool/hool in the Black Knight’s complaint. “Countour” appears only as an internal reference/catalogue term and is not used to close a rhyming couplet in the poem. So the word Chaucer does not make a rhyme with is Countour.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. None of the above

In the octosyllabic couplets of *The Book of the Duchess* Chaucer is using all of the forms you list as rhyme positions.

* wente / shente etc. is the ordinary past of *wen* ‘to go’ and is the regular rhyme
  of the poem, e.g. wente – shente.
* here is rhymed in the normal Middle English manner with there / fere / mere
  etc.
* fool is a normal  -ool rhyme of the poem, e.g. fool – cool / rule etc.
* hool = ME hol, whole, is the regular spelling/variant of *whole* and it is
  the partner of the -ool rhyme class in the poem, so Chaucer does rhyme with
  hool/whole in the same -ool set as fool.
* countour, ME countour ‘counter, reckoner, accountant’, occurs in the Duchess
  and is rhymed in the poem in the -our class, e.g. countour – tourn / toun
  etc.

Hence every item A–E is in fact used as a rhyme-word in *The Book of the Duchess*; there is no word on the list that Chaucer avoids rhyming.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the octosyllabic couplets of the Duchess Chaucer is constantly using the ordinary
end-words of his MS vocabulary as rhyming couplets.  Wente is the regular past of
‘wend’ and is rhymed e.g. with shente, Here is rhymed with there/dere etc., Fool
is the regular self-mockery of the dreamer and is rhymed with cool and with the
contemporary form hool, and Hool/hoole is indeed used in the poem as the
Middle-English partner of fool.  

Countour in the sense in which it is offered here – the ME ‘counter, reckoner,
figure’ – does not occur as a line-final, i.e. rhyming, word in the Duchess.
The word is essentially an inventory/administrative term which Chaucer reserves
for the other dream visions and for the later works, so on that list it is the only
item that is not actually put into a Duchess rhyme.  If the test is taken in the
strict ‘does the form occur as a rhymed end-word in the Duchess?’ sense the
formal set Wente / Here / Fool / Hool is all attested as rhyme-words, Countour
is not.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 0 discussion is split three ways over which of A-E, if any, is not rhymed in The Book of the Duchess.

E. Countour camp — Colleagues 1,7,8,9,10:
* Claim wente, here, fool, hool all occur as line-final rhyme words: wente ~ sente/entente/shente; here ~ there/where/dere/mere; fool ~ cool/tool/rule; hool ~ fool/cool as ME ‘whole/hale’ – the familiar fool-hool pair in the Black Knight’s complaint.
* Claim countour/counter ‘reckoner’ is not used as a line-final rhyme in the Duchess; appears only mid-line/catalogue term, reserved for later works. Spelling variation normalized, the four ordinary rhyme words are attested, countour is the only non-rhymed item.

D. Hool camp — Colleagues 3,6:
* Claim all except hool are used as rhyme words: wente:sente, here:dere/fere, fool:cool/tool, countour:mountour/doubtour/tretour/tourn.
* Claim the –ool rhyme is carried by fool/cool/tool etc., and the form hool does not occur as a rhymed line ending in the Duchess. Hool is not set up as a rhyme partner; the fool ~ cool pairing is the actual rhyme.

F. None of the above camp — Colleagues 2,4,5:
* Claim all five forms occur as rhyming end-words.
* wente ~ sente/kente/shente in rhyme royal/octosyllabic couplets.
* here ~ there/where/were/dere/fere.
* fool ~ cool/tool; hool ~ fool, ME hol/whole/hale is the regular partner in the –ool class, so hool is rhymed, indeed with fool itself.
* countour ~ mountour/doubtour/tourn/toun, used in description of the Black Knight’s lady and rhymed in ordinary couplets.

Key disagreements:
* Does countour occur as a line-final rhyme in the Duchess? E camp says no, F camp says yes with –our partners.
* Does hool occur as a line-final rhyme? D camp says no, E/F camps say yes as ME whole/hole and as partner of fool.
* Evidence cited for wente and here is broadly consistent across camps; fool is agreed rhymed, dispute is about its partner.

Unresolved: actual line-final attestations for countour vs hool in the manuscript tradition of The Book of the Duchess; whether ‘hool’ is a distinct lexical form in the poem or a scribal variant of ‘hole/whole’, and whether countour is attested at line-end at all. Need to check primary text for line-final forms.

My current belief is unsettled; the countour vs hool split hinges on manuscript verification.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 0 discussion on whether Chaucer rhymes with wente, here, fool, hool, countour in *The Book of the Duchess*.

Main split:
- E. Countour camp (Colleagues 1,10,7,8,9): wente e.g. wente/sente/entente; here e.g. here/there/dere/fere; fool e.g. fool/cool/tool; hool/hoole used as the -ool partner of fool in the Black Knight’s complaint. Countour/counter is claimed not to occur as a line-final rhyme, only mid-line/inventory use. Therefore Countour is the non-rhymed item.
- F. None of the above camp (Colleagues 2,4,5): All five forms are attested as rhyme-words. wente ~ sente/shente/kente; here ~ there/where/dere/were; fool ~ cool/tool/rule; hool/whole is the regular ME -ool partner and is rhymed, indeed with fool itself; countour ~ mountour/doubtour/tourn/toun is also claimed to be in the -our rhyme class in the Duchess description of the Black Knight’s lady.
- D. Hool camp (Colleagues 3,6): wente, here, fool, countour all occur as rhyme positions; hool in the sense offered does not occur as a rhymed line ending. The -ool rhyme is carried by fool/cool/tool, and hool is not set up as a rhyme partner in the poem. Countour is said to rhyme with its normal -our partners.

Key claims to preserve:
* wente is repeatedly cited as a regular past of wende, rhymed with sente/shente/rente.
* here is regularly line-final, rhymed with there/dere/fere/mere.
* fool is a normal -ool rhyme, e.g. fool/cool.
* hool/hoole = ME whole/hale; dispute whether it actually appears as a rhymed end-word in the Duchess vs being a theoretical rhyme partner.
* countour/counter = ME ‘reckoner’. Dispute whether it appears at all and, if so, whether it is line-final: E camp says it is absent from the couplet rhyme system; F camp says it is rhymed with mountour/doubtour/tourn etc.

Unresolved questions:
Which forms are actually attested as line-final rhyme words in the surviving manuscripts of *The Book of the Duchess*? Specifically, does countour appear in a rhymed couplet in the poem, and does hool/hoole appear as a rhymed line ending, or only as a variant of whole used elsewhere? Need to check the actual rhyme inventory rather than assumed Middle English rhyme classes.

Current belief: majority weight in round 0 favors E Countour as the non-rhymed item, with strong dissent on both hool and countour. No firm personal conclusion yet; need textual verification of countour and hool attestations.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 0 discussion about which of Wente / Here / Fool / Hool / Countour is NOT a rhyme word in The Book of the Duchess.

Public claims received:

* Wente: widely agreed as a normal ME past of wende, used in line-final rhyme. Cited pairings wente ~ sente / shente / tente / entente.
* Here: widely agreed as regular line-final rhyme. Cited pairings here ~ there / where / dere / fere / manere.
* Fool: widely agreed as regular -ool rhyme. Cited pairings fool ~ cool / tool / rule.
* Hool: split.
  - Claims it is attested as a rhyming partner of fool/cool, ME hool/hoole ‘whole, hale’ being the regular -ool partner in the poem; e.g. fool ~ hool in Black Knight’s complaint. Colleagues 2,4,5,8,9 treat hool as rhymed.
  - Claims hool in the form offered does not occur as a rhymed line ending; the -ool rhyme is carried by fool/cool/tool etc., and the specific form hool is not set up as a rhyme partner in Duchess. Colleagues 3,6 treat hool as non-rhymed.
* Countour: split.
  - Claims countour ~ counter ‘reckoner/account’ does not occur as a line-final rhyme word in Duchess; it appears at best mid-line or is absent, while the other four are attested as end-rhymes. Colleagues 1,10,7,8,9 vote E. Countour.
  - Claims countour is put into the rhyme scheme, rhymed with mountour / doubtour / tretour / tourn, and therefore is attested. Colleagues 2,4,5,6 vote F. None of the above. Colleague 3 votes D. Hool and accepts countour as rhymed.

Competing answers:
E. Countour – 5 colleagues, 1,10,7,8,9.
F. None of the above – 3 colleagues, 2,4,5.
D. Hool – 2 colleagues, 3,6.

Unresolved factual points I need to keep:
* Does the form hool/hoole actually occur line-final in Book of the Duchess, or is it a conflation with whole/hale? If hool = whole, is the spelling used in the MS and rhymed?
* Does countour/counter actually occur line-final in Book of the Duchess, e.g., countour ~ mountour/doubtour? The E camp says it appears only mid-line / not at all; the F camp says it is rhymed in the -our class.

No prior belief to revise. Current leaning is uncertain; majority weight is on E Countour, but the strong counter-claim that all five are attested and that hool is the non-rhyme item complicates. Need verification of actual line-final attestations for hool and countour in the Duchess text before committing.

* Does hool/hoole/whole occur line-finally as a rhymed word, and if so is it rhymed with fool or with cool? Some colleagues treat hool = whole as the regular rhyme partner of fool; others say the form hool never appears as a rhymed ending, with the -ool rhyme being fool~cool only.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 0 discussion shows a split on what, if any, of the five forms is not used as a rhyme-end in *The Book of the Duchess*.

Common ground:
* wente is accepted by all as a regular rhyme-end, e.g. wente ~ sente / shente / rente.
* here is accepted by all as a regular rhyme-end, e.g. here ~ there / dere / fere / where.
* fool is accepted by all as a regular -ool rhyme-end, e.g. fool ~ cool / tool / rule.

Disagreement:
* Hool. Colleagues 3 and 6 claim hool / hoole ‘whole, hale’ does not occur as a rhymed line ending in the Duchess; the -ool rhyme is carried by fool / cool / tool etc. Colleagues 4,5,8 argue hool is the Middle English partner of fool in the -ool class and is indeed rhymed, even with fool itself.
* Countour. Colleagues 1,10,7,8,9 argue countour ~ counter ‘reckoner, account’ does not occur as a line-final rhyme in the Duchess; it appears only medially or not at all, while wente/here/fool/hool are all attested as rhyme words. Colleagues 2,4,5 argue countour is put into the -our rhyme class in the poem, e.g. countour ~ mountour / tourn / doubtour, and thus all five forms A-E are rhymed.

Overall weight in round 0 is toward E. Countour: five colleagues explicitly pick E, two pick D. Hool, and three pick F. None of the above. The F camp rests on the claim that hool/whole is part of the normal -ool set and that countour is also rhymed with -our partners in the Duchess.

Unresolved: whether the form hool actually occurs as a rhyme-end in the Duchess manuscript tradition, and whether countour/counter occurs at line-end at all in this work versus later dream visions / Canterbury Tales. The distinction between ‘form appears in the poem’ and ‘form appears as a rhyme-end’ is key, as is normalisation of spelling for countour/counter and hool/hoole/hol.

My current lean is to the majority E position, with the caveat that the hool claim needs direct textual verification; if hool is indeed unattested as a rhyme-end, D would be the correct non-rhymer and the F argument collapses.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which of Wente, Here, Fool, Hool, Countour is not used by Chaucer as a rhyming line-end in The Book of the Duchess, or whether all five are used.

Round-0 positions:
* Wente: unanimously claimed rhymed, e.g. wente ~ sente / shente / entente.
* Here: unanimously claimed rhymed, e.g. here ~ there / dere / fere / were.
* Fool: unanimously claimed rhymed, e.g. fool ~ cool / tool / rule.
* Hool: split. Colleagues 3,6 argue hool is not set up as a rhyme partner in the Duchess; the -ool class is carried by fool/cool/tool and the form hool does not occur as a rhymed line ending. Colleagues 1,4,5,7,8,9 argue hool = ME hol/hoole ‘whole, hale’ is the regular partner of the -ool rhyme family and is attested as rhymed, indeed with fool itself, in the Black Knight’s complaint.
* Countour: split. Colleagues 1,7,8,9,10 argue countour / counteour ‘reckoner, counter’ does not occur as a line-final rhyming word in the Duchess; it appears only mid-line or not at all, and the -our class in the poem is not realized by that lexeme. Colleagues 2,4,5 argue countour is put into the rhyme scheme and rhymed with mountour/doubtour/tourn/toum etc., so it is used.
* None of the above: colleagues 2,4,5 claim all five forms are attested as rhyming end-words, with hool identified with whole and countour identified with the -our class.

Current understanding: Wente, Here and Fool are uncontroversial rhyming end-words. The crux is hool vs countour. Majority of the colleagues in round 0, 1,7,8,9,10, i.e. five votes for E Countour, argue hool is effectively the ME whole and is used in the fool/hool rhyme, whereas countour is the odd one out. A substantial minority, 2,4,5, claim both hool and countour are rhymed, leading to F None of the above. A smaller minority, 3,6, claims hool is the non-rhyming item.

Unresolved factual checks needed: actual line-final attestations of hool/hoole in the Duchess and of countour/counteour as a rhyme word. If hool does not appear as a line ending, D Hool would be correct; if countour does not appear as a line ending, E Countour would be correct; if both appear, F None of the above would be correct.

I am currently leaning with the majority E Countour, pending verification that hool/whole is indeed used in rhyme in the poem, while countour is not attested as a Duchess rhyme word.
